name: David Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a trainee jumbo operator at the Ironbark Deep nickel mine, underground. A jumbo is a drilling rig on wheels with two or three long arms, and we use it to drill the face of a new tunnel so the charge-up crew can blast it forward another few metres. Shift starts at six, we drive down the decline, which is the big spiral tunnel, and I spend the day drilling the pattern with my trainer, Pete, watching every hole.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making the mine bigger, literally. Every round we blast is ground nobody's ever seen. What wears me out is the noise and the water, and that I'm still slow at lining up the booms, so Pete takes over on the tricky faces. On my days off I do fencing jobs with my uncle Sam on his land and the farms around, with his old skid steer, and that's what keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world needed a reality check. Hard work still counts. I'd say it at the pub and at my uncle's table and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that's the best case for me. I've got a well-paid job, I'm learning a skill, and Leila and I can get married next year like we planned. I'd keep building towards owning land of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep drilling, keep getting better so Pete stops grabbing the controls. Keep doing fencing jobs on weekends with Sam, which brings in a bit extra. We've got about nine months of costs saved, and I'd keep putting money aside for a block of land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a good season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to write up quotes for the fencing jobs, because my spelling is terrible. It's handy for that, but I wouldn't trust it with anything important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does owning land mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's what my family's always done when they could. My grandfather had goats and a few acres, and my uncle still does. You can't lose land the way you can lose a job.

S0.say: I'd say the world needed a reality check and hard work still counts. I'd say it at the pub and at my uncle's table and leave it at that.
S0.think: That's the best case for me, with a well-paid job, a skill to learn, and a wedding next year. I'd keep building towards owning land.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and improving so his trainer stops taking over. Keeps doing weekend fencing jobs with his uncle and saving towards a block of land.
S0.quote: You can't lose land the way you can lose a job.
S0.fieldNote: David builds his security from family, land and a weekend trade, not just his mine wage. He uses AI for small jobs like quotes but doesn't trust it with anything important. His values shape his plan: work hard, marry, own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when apprenticeships matter more than ever. Young people should learn a real trade instead of waiting for someone to look after them. At work I'd say the same to the other trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the jumbo could go automatic fairly soon. Some mines already have rigs that drill the pattern by themselves. So I'd want a trade that fixes the machines, not one that drives them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen a couple of the lads do it, I'd apply for a heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship, which is a mechanic for big machines, on site. The pay drops for a few years, but our savings and the fencing work would cover it. I'd keep the wedding plans as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's a clear path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see a couple of others do it first. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to jump at the first thing the company says. They told us the new ventilation system would be perfect and we spent a month in the heat. If Mitch and Jordan go first and it works, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Leila feel about the pay cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a bookkeeper, so she'd have a spreadsheet out before I finished the sentence. She'd want to see it add up. I think it would, with the fencing money.

S1.say: I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever, and young people should learn a real trade instead of waiting to be looked after. I'd tell the other trainees the same.
S1.think: The jumbo could go automatic soon, because some mines already have rigs that drill by themselves. I'd want a trade that fixes the machines, not one that drives them.
S1.do: Waits until a couple of colleagues have tried it, then applies for an on-site heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship. Covers the pay cut with savings and weekend fencing income and keeps the wedding plans.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, seeing a clear path.
S1.quote: She's a bookkeeper, so she'd have a spreadsheet out before I finished the sentence.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional faith in apprenticeships fits neatly with the steady scenario. He waits for proof from workmates, based on the company's past over-promises. His partner's practical eye and the fencing income make the pay cut feel manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mistake to let it rip this fast, and that the companies doing it should carry the cost, not taxpayers. At work I'd say we stick together and look after our own. I don't post online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it hits everything at once. The jumbo, the fitter trade, and even fencing, if a robot can dig post holes. The land would still be there, but I'd be wondering what I'd do on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as they'd have me and save every cent. We'd do a small wedding, at my uncle's place, and skip the honeymoon. I'd lean on family, Sam and my parents, before I'd go to the government, and I'd use the savings to put a deposit on that block while land is still cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we've got savings and family, but a heavy feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, would you still start the fitter apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. A fitter apprenticeship is four years, so I'd finish it after it no longer mattered. In two years I'd rather earn the jumbo money and buy the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy land in this picture, of all of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything else is up in the air, at least you can grow food and keep a few animals. My grandfather did that through some bad years. It's not a business plan, it's a roof and a garden.

S2.say: I'd say it's a mistake to let it happen this fast, and the companies doing it should carry the cost, not taxpayers. At work I'd say we stick together and look after our own.
S2.think: It hits everything at once: the jumbo, the fitter trade and even fencing. The land would still be there, but I'd wonder what I'd do on it.
S2.do: Works and saves as long as the job lasts, holds a small wedding at his uncle's place and skips the honeymoon. Leans on family before government and uses savings for a deposit on a block of land.
S2.feel: Anxious and heavy, but not panicked thanks to savings and family.
S2.quote: It's not a business plan, it's a roof and a garden.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning he drops the apprenticeship as too slow and turns to land as a fallback. Family comes before any government support in his thinking. He'd still marry, but smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight, so start now: apprenticeships, family businesses, whatever keeps people working. I'd talk to the younger guys about not wasting it. At the pub I'd probably be the one saying it isn't the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd squeeze in most of a trade and a few years of the fencing business. It wouldn't last forever, but it would get us through the first years of being married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the fitter apprenticeship, if a couple of others had done it, because I could finish most of it in time. Sam and I would buy a second-hand mini excavator for the fencing and small earthworks, so the business could take bigger jobs. We'd keep the wedding as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, but uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two, I'm just holding on. In five, I can actually build something: a trade ticket and a small business with Sam. Even if robots come for that too, I'd have been my own boss for a while, and that matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying an excavator a risk if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but it's a small machine and we'd buy it second-hand. If it pays for itself in three years, it doesn't matter much what happens after. And you can always sell a machine.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight, so start now with apprenticeships and family businesses. At the pub I'd be the one saying it isn't the end of the world.
S3.think: I'd squeeze in most of a trade and a few years of the fencing business. It wouldn't last forever, but it would get us through the first married years.
S3.do: Starts the fitter apprenticeship once others have, and buys a second-hand mini excavator with his uncle to grow the fencing and earthworks business. Keeps the wedding as planned.
S3.quote: Even if robots come for that too, I'd have been my own boss for a while, and that matters to me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts him from holding on to building, through a trade and a family business. He weighs the excavator purchase carefully and expects it to pay back fast. Being his own boss carries weight beyond the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this the right way: train young people properly, keep families working, and don't let anyone get lazy waiting for handouts. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. Ten years is a full apprenticeship plus a business. I'd be thirty-seven, married, with land, a trade and maybe a couple of kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep drilling and save, get married, and once a couple of the lads had gone ahead, start the fitter apprenticeship. Sam and I would grow the fencing slowly, no big purchases yet. We'd probably buy the land in year two or three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal life with a deadline somewhere far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change any plans in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Wedding next year, kids in a few years, land when we can. Ten years is enough time that I don't think God needs us to rearrange anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger cousins, the teenagers. They'd be starting work right when it all lands, and they'd need to choose well. I'd want to talk to them about trades and land now, not later.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly: train young people, keep families working and don't let people wait for handouts. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.
S4.think: I'd be fine, because ten years is a full apprenticeship plus a business. At thirty-seven I'd be married, with land, a trade and maybe kids.
S4.do: Keeps drilling, saves and gets married in the first year, then starts the fitter apprenticeship once workmates have tried it. Grows the fencing business slowly and plans to buy land in year two or three.
S4.feel: Calm, like normal life with a far-off deadline.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time that I don't think God needs us to rearrange anything.
S4.fieldNote: The decade-long picture leaves his life plan intact. His faith colours how he talks about it, with a quiet confidence. His worry turns to younger relatives entering work just as the change lands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to finish a trade or build the business. What would help is the companies paying for real apprenticeships and helping small family businesses get started, not just sending everyone a cheque. People need something to do with their hands and their days.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. When you've drilled a round and the face blasts clean, the whole crew walks in to look at it. I don't know what a man does with that feeling if a robot drilled it.

headlineQuote: When you've drilled a round and the face blasts clean, the whole crew walks in to look at it.
portrait: David Farah is a 27-year-old trainee jumbo operator at an underground nickel mine, still slow at lining up the drilling booms and learning from his trainer Pete. He lives with his partner Leila, a bookkeeper, they plan to marry next year, and they have about nine months of costs saved. On weekends he does fencing jobs with his uncle, and his long-term goal is to own land. He waits for proof before changing course and believes in apprenticeships over handouts. He stays calm in most pictures, becomes anxious only when AGI arrives in two years, and turns to land, family and a small business as his fallback.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to finish a trade or build the fencing business.
whatWouldHelp: Companies paying for real apprenticeships and helping small family businesses start, rather than just sending everyone a cheque.
